article.headline: Three.wasm's Fake Benchmark Illuminates What WebAssembly Can and Cannot Do
article.lede: On April 1, 2026, Ricardo Cabello — better known online as mrdoob, the creator of three.js — published three.wasm, an April Fools prank billed as a '10KB binary rendering 3D graphics at 480+ fps.' The performance display was a random number generator; an actual measurement on an Apple M4 Pro returned about 15 fps. The joke worked because every technical claim was a precise distortion of something real.
article.body:
On April 1, 2026, Ricardo Cabello published three.wasm to a prompt endorsement from @threejs — 'The future of Three.js is WebAssembly' — an account he also controls. The repository's README promised liberation from *garbage collection* pauses, *JIT* warm-up delays, and even from JavaScript itself, and was archived the following day. The .wasm binary is technically real: 10,913 bytes of *AssemblyScript*-compiled code that rotates 36 vertices for a single cube. What is not real is the frame-rate figure. A single JavaScript expression generates a random integer between 460 and 499 each frame and displays it as a measurement. A user who actually timed the demo on a modern laptop reported roughly 15 fps — the expected ceiling for a render loop synchronized to the display via *requestAnimationFrame* doing minimal work.

**WebAssembly** is a binary instruction format designed to run inside browsers at speeds closer to compiled machine code than JavaScript typically achieves. Its fixed numeric type system eliminates runtime type-inference overhead, and its ahead-of-time compilation removes the latency of *JIT* warm-up on first execution. For compute-bound tasks — physics solvers, matrix math, geometry processing — Wasm can outperform JavaScript by a factor of two to eight. A 2019 academic study using *SPEC CPU* benchmarks found Wasm 1.45 to 1.55 times slower than truly native compiled code on average, however, with worst-case slowdowns reaching 2.5 times. 'Faster than native' is accurate only if 'native' means JavaScript — not machine code compiled with a full native toolchain.

The joke's deeper target is a real pattern. Jonathan Hale of Wonderland Engine, a competing *WebGL* framework, published a technical post the following day arguing that the dominant bottleneck in WebGL rendering is not JavaScript computation but *draw calls* — the commands sent from a webpage to the browser's graphics thread, each validated and marshalled to the GPU driver. That overhead is identical whether the calling code is JavaScript or WebAssembly. Cabello has said in interviews that three.js applications tend to choke on draw call count, not on the speed of matrix arithmetic. Wasm is effective where the CPU is the bottleneck; it helps little when the bottleneck is the graphics API boundary.

Cabello's sense of humor has long been part of his engineering identity. Three.js grew from the Barcelona *demoscene* — a subculture defined by producing technically impressive real-time visuals in programs of absurd smallness — and he has described his ambition for the web as making it 'more demoscene-ish.' Three.wasm earned 537 stars before the repo was archived. Its most memorable issue report came from a user announcing a venture-backed project requiring support for 'two spinning cubes.' The prank succeeds because its half-truths are real: the binary is genuinely 10KB, AssemblyScript does compile to optimized Wasm, and the broader case for Wasm on the web is legitimate. What Cabello lampoons is the gap between capability and the marketing language that invariably precedes it.

concepts.definition: A binary instruction format that runs inside web browsers at speeds closer to compiled code than JavaScript typically achieves. Programs in C++, Rust, or AssemblyScript are compiled to Wasm, which the browser executes with ahead-of-time compilation and no garbage collector.

An automatic memory-management process in languages like JavaScript that periodically reclaims memory from objects no longer in use. The pauses it introduces — GC pauses — can cause visible hitches in real-time graphics applications.

A technique JavaScript engines use to compile frequently executed code to machine code at runtime rather than interpreting it line by line. JIT adds a warm-up delay on first run, as the engine must observe code behavior before it can optimize; subsequent executions are faster.

A programming language with TypeScript-like syntax that compiles to WebAssembly rather than JavaScript. It lets developers write code resembling TypeScript while targeting the Wasm runtime, without switching to C++ or Rust.

A browser API that schedules a JavaScript callback to run immediately before the next screen repaint, synchronizing render loops to the display's refresh rate — typically 60, 90, or 120 Hz. Render loops using it are naturally capped at that rate, making a sustained display of 480+ fps physically impossible on most monitors.

A standardized suite of compute-intensive programs maintained by the Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation, widely used in academic and industry research to compare CPU performance across language runtimes and architectures. Results are considered more representative of real-world workloads than narrow micro-benchmarks.

A JavaScript API for rendering 2D and 3D graphics in a web browser using the host machine's GPU. The browser acts as an intermediary, validating draw commands before passing them to the underlying graphics driver — overhead that neither JavaScript nor WebAssembly can bypass.

Commands issued by CPU-side code to a graphics API — here, WebGL — instructing the GPU to render a batch of geometry. Each draw call crosses from the webpage into the browser's graphics thread and incurs validation and driver overhead; a scene with many small draw calls is typically slower than one using fewer, larger ones.

A computer subculture, most active in Europe from the 1980s onward, dedicated to creating technically impressive real-time audio-visual programs — typically within severe size constraints such as 4KB or 64KB. Three.js creator Ricardo Cabello came up through the Barcelona demoscene, and its ethos of doing more with less is visible in the library's design.

repos.summary: An April Fools 2026 satirical project by three.js creator Ricardo Cabello — a real 10KB WebAssembly binary compiled from AssemblyScript that rotates a single cube using WebGL2, packaged with a fake fps counter outputting random numbers between 460 and 499. The joke targets the category of Wasm announcements that overstate performance gains. Archived April 2, 2026, with 537 stars.

The most widely used JavaScript library for WebGL 3D graphics, with over 112,000 GitHub stars. Created by Ricardo Cabello in 2010, it provides a high-level scene graph, cameras, materials, and loaders over the raw WebGL API. Its minified core is roughly 175KB — the size that three.wasm satirically claimed to replace with a 10KB binary.

article.fact_check: The '480+ fps' figure is fabricated: the source code generates a random integer between 460 and 499 and displays it as a frame-rate measurement. A user's actual timing on an M4 Pro MacBook returned roughly 15 fps — the expected ceiling for a display-refresh-synchronized loop doing minimal work. 'Faster than native' is a deliberate ambiguity: Wasm can outperform JavaScript on compute-bound tasks, but peer-reviewed SPEC CPU benchmarks place it 1.45–1.55× slower than truly native compiled code on average. The '8× faster' headline in the repository description has no supporting benchmark and appears to be satirical inflation of the kind of language used in real Wasm announcements.
